spots.note: Monsoon-only falls in a forested gorge on the Harsul road; the rock is slippery, only worth it July to September.

spots.name: Harihar Fort
spots.note: Near vertical steps cut into a basalt thumb, exposed and famous; go early on a weekday and never on wet rock.

name: Tuljapur
tagline: Tulja Bhavani, Shivaji's family goddess, on a Balaghat ridge
festival: Sep/Oct: Navratri fair at the Tulja Bhavani temple

why.winter: Dec-Feb is 12-31 C at 650 m and the stepped temple courtyards are quiet enough to sit in for an hour.
why.summer: Apr-May runs 41-43 C on bare Balaghat rock with almost no shade between the bus stand and the temple.
why.monsoon: Jul-Sep gets around 700 mm, the ridge greens up briefly and Navratri crowds start building in September.
why.autumn: Navratri turns the town into a nine-night fair of palanquins and drums, with no spare rooms anywhere.

vibe: Kuldevata pilgrims from across Maharashtra, coconut and garland stalls, and plain bhakta-niwas rooms
hub: Buses every half hour from Solapur 45 km and Dharashiv 20 km; Solapur is the railhead, Naldurg 35 km

spots.name: Gomukh Tirth
spots.note: Spring-fed kund below the temple where pilgrims bathe before darshan; the steps are slippery, go at first light.

spots.name: Naldurg Fort
spots.note: Huge basalt water fort where the Nar and Madi falls pour over the dam wall; both only run after heavy rain.

spots.name: Dharashiv Caves
spots.note: Seven rock-cut Jain and Buddhist caves in a scrub valley outside Dharashiv; take a rickshaw, there is no signage.

spots.name: Papanash Tirth
spots.note: Old bathing tank a short walk from the temple on the pradakshina route; quietest in the afternoon lull after 1 pm.

spots.name: Chintamani
spots.note: Stone in the temple precinct where devotees put a question to the goddess and wait; the queue is short at dawn.

name: Velas (Turtle Village)
tagline: Olive ridley hatchlings released on a Konkan village beach
festival: Feb/Mar: Velas turtle festival, hatchling releases at dawn and dusk

why.winter: Dec-Jan is calm and empty, the nesting has already happened but the hatchlings have not emerged yet.
why.summer: March into early April is the peak release window; by May it is 35 C, sticky, and the season is done.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the beach is battered by surf, the homestays shut and the last unmetalled stretch in turns to mud.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is pleasant and near-deserted, good for the Bankot fort walk but with no turtles to be seen.

vibe: Sahyadri Nisarg Mitra homestays, a mattress on the floor and thali meals; families, birders, volunteers
hub: Khed railhead 70 km or Mangaon 87 km, then ST bus via Bankot; book a Velas homestay before you travel

spots.name: Velas Beach
spots.note: Grey-sand bay with the fenced turtle hatchery; releases are at dawn from late February to April, stay behind the rope.

spots.name: Bankot Fort
spots.note: Small hilltop fort over the mouth of the Savitri; open, free and shadeless, best an hour before sunset.

spots.name: Harihareshwar
spots.note: Shiva town across the Bagmandla ferry with a rock pradakshina round the headland; check ferry timings before you set out.

spots.name: Kelshi
spots.note: Konkan village of the Mahalaxmi temple and the Yakub Baba dargah with a wide empty beach; the road in is very narrow.

spots.name: Anjarle
spots.note: Kadyavarcha Ganpati sits on a cliff above the creek and an empty beach; the bridge saves the old ferry, no bus after dark.

name: Vengurla
tagline: Cashew-and-fish Konkan town with empty coves near Goa

why.winter: Nov-Feb is the season: 20-32 C, flat calm mornings and Sagareshwar or Mochemad sands to yourself while Goa heaves an hour south.
why.summer: Mar-Apr is hot and sticky but mango and cashew harvest fills the town with trade; May is 34 C and airless before the rains break.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep is full Konkan monsoon: around 3000 mm, rough surf and shuttered homestays; a lovely coast road but not beach weather.
why.autumn: Oct dries out fast and the sea settles; homestays reopen and you get green hills plus swimmable water before the season proper.

vibe: Fishing-family homestays under coconut and cashew; long-stay quiet-seekers, no shacks and no party scene
hub: Konkan Railway to Kudal or Sawantwadi (25-30 km), then bus or rickshaw; Goa's Mopa airport is about 60 km

spots.name: Sagareshwar Beach
spots.note: Vengurla's own crescent under casuarina with a Shiva temple at one end; no shacks at all, carry water and cash.

spots.name: Vengurla Rocks
spots.note: Offshore rocks with a lighthouse and nesting seabirds; hire a boat at the port, they only run in calm weather.

spots.name: Nivati Beach
spots.note: Empty cove below the ruined Nivati fort on the headland; dolphin boats leave from Bhogwe next door, no food stalls.

spots.name: Redi Ganesh Temple
spots.note: Two-armed Ganesh dug out of a laterite mine in the 1970s; the red mining beach and Yashwantgad fort are alongside.

spots.name: Shiroda Velagar Beach
spots.note: Three km of straight sand behind casuarina, almost always empty; the current is strong, do not swim past the break.

name: Loktak Lake
tagline: Floating phumdi islands, world's only floating park

why.winter: Best season: clear water, migratory birds, easiest sangai deer sightings on the phumdis.
why.summer: March-April still good for boating; by May it turns hot and humid ahead of the rains.
why.monsoon: The lake floods significantly, phumdis break loose and drift, park access often restricted.
why.autumn: October water is still settling post-monsoon, boat trips resume through the month.

vibe: Quiet stilted fishing villages; check current travel advisories before going.
hub: Fly Imphal, 1h drive to Moirang. ILP + PAP; check advisories.

spots.name: Keibul Lamjao National Park
spots.note: The floating park and last home of the sangai deer; climb the Pabot hill watch tower at dawn for any chance of one.

spots.name: Sendra Island
spots.note: Hillock in the middle of the lake with a tourist lodge and cafe; the rings of floating phumdi read best at sunrise.

spots.name: INA Memorial, Moirang
spots.note: Where the INA flag first flew on Indian soil in 1944, with a small museum of the Imphal campaign; an hour is enough.

spots.name: Thanga
spots.note: Fishing village of stilt houses on a lake island; the homestays here arrange the two hour boat out among the phumdi.

spots.name: Karang Island
spots.note: The largest island in the lake, reached by shared boat from Thanga; walking the ridge round it takes about two hours.

name: Shirui (Ukhrul)
tagline: Tangkhul Naga village under the 2,835 m peak where the Shirui lily blooms
festival: May: Shirui Lily Festival at Ukhrul, usually the third or fourth week; the lily itself flowers late May to mid June

why.winter: Dec-Feb is dry and sharp, frost on the ridge and nights near 0 C, but the 3 h climb to Shirui Kashong gives the clearest views of the year across the Myanmar hills
why.summer: April brings rhododendron on the upper trail and by the last week of May the lily flowers; festival week fills every bed in Ukhrul, so book early or camp at Shirui
why.monsoon: June still shows lilies in mist but the rain sets in; Jul-Aug the Imphal-Ukhrul road slips and the trail is mud with no view, so skip; September clears slowly
why.autumn: Oct-Nov are the calm months: harvested terraces, cold clear mornings, the peak in 3 h without a crowd, and Longpi's black pottery village up the Jessami road

vibe: Tangkhul homestays in Shirui and small hotels in Ukhrul town, 15 km back; evenings are church choirs, rice beer and an early night
hub: Fly to Imphal; shared Sumos to Ukhrul take about 3 h (83 km), then a local taxi or Jessami-bound jeep 15 km to Shirui

name: Tamenglong (Barak Waterfalls)
tagline: Rongmei Naga hill town of orange orchards, Barak river falls and Tharon cave
festival: Dec: Tamenglong Orange Festival, orchard stalls and Rongmei dance in town

why.winter: Dec-Feb is dry and cool with 5 C mornings: orange harvest in the orchards below town, the Orange Festival in December, and clear days for Tharon cave 27 km out
why.summer: Mar-Apr are dry and hazy from jhum fires; the Barak falls thin to threads but the road is at its best and the town is empty of visitors; May storms begin
why.monsoon: June rain turns the Barak falls into a roar, but Jul-Aug are the wettest months of a 2,600 mm year and the hill road from Khongsang slips, so wait; September dries out slowly
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the window: the falls still full, the Barak gorge and Zeilad lake green, the Imphal road repaired, and the first oranges on the trees by late November

vibe: A tin-roofed ridge town of churches and Sumo stands; a few lodges, a circuit house and homestays; the market shuts by 6 pm
hub: Fly to Imphal; shared Sumos leave around 7 am and take about 5 h via NH37 to Khongsang and up the hill road (140 km)

name: Willong Khullen
tagline: Maram Naga ridge village ringed by 7 m menhirs no one counts the same way twice

why.winter: Dec-Feb is dry, cold and clear, 2 C mornings on the ridge; the menhirs stand in stubble fields and the 39 km interior road from Maram is at its firmest for a Sumo
why.summer: Mar-Apr is dry with peach and plum blossom in the village and haze from jhum burning; May brings the first storms and the road starts to soften
why.monsoon: June is wet but passable in a jeep; Jul-Aug turn the Maram-Peren road into mud with slips, so wait; September is green, the paddy tall around the stones, roads drying
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is harvest time: ripe paddy up to the menhirs, cold clear mornings, and the village at its most open to visitors before the winter

vibe: A Maram village of tin roofs and paddy, no hotel: ask the village authority for a room or sleep back in Senapati; dusk empties the site
hub: Fly to Imphal; Kohima buses or Sumos to Maram Centre on NH2 (3 h), then 39 km on NH129A towards Peren by hired car or jeep

name: Baghmara (Balpakram gateway)
tagline: Someshwari river town under the Balpakram plateau

why.winter: Nov-Feb is dry at 12-28 C and the only sane time to make the 50 km run up to the Balpakram plateau and back.
why.summer: Mar-May is 35 C and sticky down at 25 m by the Bangladesh border, and pre-monsoon storms wreck the hill roads.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the Garo hill roads slide and the Someshwari runs brown and fast; getting in or out becomes guesswork.
why.autumn: October is green and quiet, village Wangala drums start up, and the track towards Balpakram is drying out.

vibe: District-town lodges and a tourist rest house; shared jeeps full of traders, and you are the only outsider
hub: Shared Sumo from Tura 4-5 h via Siju; Balpakram needs a hired jeep from here, there is no bus to the park

spots.name: Balpakram National Park
spots.note: Cliff-edged plateau the Garos call the land of the dead; hire a jeep for the day in Baghmara, no bus and no food up top.

spots.name: Baghmara Pitcher Plant Sanctuary
spots.note: Small hillside reserve of wild Nepenthes khasiana; ask at the forest office in town, the gate is often shut.

spots.name: Simsang River
spots.note: The Simsang, called Someshwari further downstream; the sandbanks below town are the evening walk, no swimming in monsoon.

spots.name: Wari Chora
spots.note: Emerald canyon between sheer cliffs, reached by jeep then a boat and a wade; go with a village guide, not in high water.

name: Cherrapunji (Sohra)
tagline: Wettest place on earth: waterfalls, canyons, caves

why.winter: Dry and clear, good canyon and Nohkalikai Falls views, though the water flow itself is thin.
why.summer: Warming up, waterfalls still decent, dry trails good for root-bridge treks before the rains.
why.monsoon: Holds the world rainfall record here. Dramatic falls but near-zero visibility and landslide-shut roads.
why.autumn: Sweet spot: monsoon just broke, falls are at their fullest, skies finally clearing.

vibe: Small Khasi villages, guesthouse guides, same trekkers doing the falls circuit.
hub: 1.5h shared taxi from Shillong (3h from Guwahati). No ILP.

spots.name: Nohkalikai Falls
spots.note: India's tallest plunge falls seen from a paid terrace; cloud swallows it after 10 am, so come early or in October.

spots.name: Wei Sawdong Falls
spots.note: Three turquoise tiers down steep bamboo ladders below the road; small village fee, and not worth it in heavy rain.

spots.name: Mawsmai Cave
spots.note: Lit limestone passage of about 150 m with two tight squeezes; ticket at the gate, long queues on a Sunday.

spots.name: Arwah Lumshynna Cave
spots.note: Fossil-studded cave at the end of a short forest walk, quieter than Mawsmai; a guide is compulsory and gates shut early.

spots.name: Nohsngithiang (Seven Sisters) Falls
spots.note: Seven ribbons over the Mawsmai cliff into the Bangladesh plains; they only run in rain, and the light is best late.

spots.name: Thangkharang Park
spots.note: Cliff garden facing Khoh Ramhah, the giant cone rock, and the plains beyond; small fee, gates close about 4 pm.

name: Dawki & Shnongpdeng
tagline: Glass-clear Umngot river: boating, cliff camps, border

why.winter: Peak clarity: the Umngot turns glass-clear turquoise, boats look like they float on air.
why.summer: March-April still fairly clear; by May pre-monsoon showers start muddying the river.
why.monsoon: River runs brown and fast, most camps shut down: skip this window entirely.
why.autumn: October water is still settling from monsoon silt, better from November onward.

vibe: River-camp bonfires, kayaking by day, cheap tents by the water, easy to meet people.
hub: 2h shared taxi from Shillong, 4-5h from Guwahati. No ILP.

spots.name: Dawki Suspension Bridge
spots.note: Single span hung over the Umngot in 1932 and still carrying border trucks; walk it early before the queue builds.

spots.name: Borhill Falls
spots.note: Falls dropping straight into the Umngot, reached only by boat from Shnongpdeng; the boat is priced whole, so share it.

spots.name: Dawki Zero Point
spots.note: The India side of the road crossing to Tamabil in Bangladesh; you may walk up and look, carry ID and do not photograph.

spots.name: Nongjrong
spots.note: Ridge above Pynursla where cloud fills the whole valley at sunrise; leave by 4 am, the last stretch of road is rough.

name: Jowai (Nartiang & Krangsuri)
tagline: Jaintia monolith field, a Shakti Peetha and blue Krangsuri pools
festival: Jul: Behdienkhlam

why.winter: Dec-Feb is 5-18 C, dry and clear, and Nartiang's monolith field and Durga temple are yours alone before ten.
why.summer: March-April is warm and green and Krangsuri holds its turquoise colour right up until the first heavy rains.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep is brutal Jaintia rain, but Behdienkhlam in July is worth accepting it, if you expect to be soaked all day.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the cleanest window: waterfalls still full from the rains, roads dry and the paddy terraces going gold.

vibe: Pnar market town with plain hotels, few visitors beyond waterfall day-trippers, river walks along the Myntdu
hub: Shillong 64 km, shared sumos from Iewduh about 2 h; Umroi airport 85 km; no railway anywhere near

spots.name: Nartiang Monoliths
spots.note: The densest field of Jaintia menhirs anywhere, some 8 m tall, in a shaded yard; free, ten minutes off the main road.

spots.name: Krang Suri Falls
spots.note: Blue pool under a broad falls with a stepped path and rails; small entry fee, swimming allowed, packed on Sundays.

spots.name: Nartiang Durga Temple
spots.note: Low wooden Shakti Peetha of the Jaintia kings with its old sacrifice pit; Durga Puja here draws the whole district.

spots.name: Tyrshi Falls
spots.note: Falls at the head of a paddy bowl with a walkway down to the base; the valley view beats the falls except after rain.

spots.name: Syntu Ksiar
spots.note: Slow loop of the Myntdu below town with rowing boats and a bank path; this is where Jowai walks in the evening.

name: Laitlum Canyons (Rasong)
tagline: Cloud-filled amphitheatre with a stone stairway down to Rasong
festival: Nov: Ka Pomblang Nongkrem dance at Smit

why.winter: Dec-Feb skies are clear and cold at 1,790 m: you see the whole gorge out to the Bangladesh plains, and the rim wind cuts hard by 4 pm
why.summer: Mar-Apr stay green and quiet; from late April storms build after lunch and May turns properly wet, so be back up from Rasong before 3 pm
why.monsoon: Jun-Jul is landslide season, the rim sits inside white cloud and the wet steps are lethal, so wait. Aug eases, Sep is the cloud show
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the best of the year: clean air, green grass, cloud pouring over the rim at dawn, Shillong day crowds only after noon

vibe: Camera day-trippers until sunset, then nothing; you sleep in Smit or Shillong, or in a Rasong village homestay below the steps
hub: 24 km from Shillong via Smit: shared taxi to Smit, then a local cab or a 6 km walk; last ride back around 4 pm

name: Mawlynnong
tagline: Asia's cleanest village: root bridge, bamboo skywalk

why.winter: Dry paths, clear skies: the Sky View bamboo tower shows Bangladesh's plains below.
why.summer: Warm, green, fewer tourists, though afternoon showers creep in by May.
why.monsoon: Some of India's heaviest rain falls right here. Leeches, slick paths, zero views.
why.autumn: October is transitional: trails drying out, village looking its lush best.

vibe: Homestay evenings with Khasi families, mostly day-trippers, quiet overnight stays.
hub: 1h from Dawki, 2.5h shared taxi from Shillong. No ILP.

spots.name: Riwai Living Root Bridge
spots.note: Single span of woven ficus roots over a stream at Riwai; small fee, and get there before the Shillong taxis at 11.

spots.name: Sky View Bamboo Tower
spots.note: Eighty foot bamboo scaffold looking over the Bangladesh plains; pay at the base, it sways, a few people up at a time.

spots.name: Maw Ryngkew Sharatia (Balancing Rock)
spots.note: Boulder poised on a tiny stone that Khasis hold sacred; five minutes off the village lane, small fee at the path.

spots.name: Church of the Epiphany
spots.note: Stone and timber village church over a century old, still the middle of Sunday here; the door is open on weekdays.

name: Mawphanlur
tagline: Grassy knoll village of tiny lakes and kayaks at 1,850 m

why.winter: Dec-Feb is crisp and empty: near-frost mornings, mirror ponds for a slow paddle, and bonfire evenings at the village guesthouses.
why.summer: Mar-Apr gives clear ridge walks and wildflowers on the knolls; May opens the big pre-monsoon downpours, so keep plans loose.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug sits in rain and fog for days on end; the grass is at its greenest but you will see almost none of it, come later.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is peak: rain-rinsed green hills, kayak-calm ponds and long easy ridge walks in shirtsleeve sunshine.

vibe: Village-run guesthouses on bare green hilltops; Shillong weekenders paddle, solo walkers get whole ridges to themselves
hub: 78 km from Shillong via Mairang, 2.5 h; take a Nongstoin sumo to the turn-off and a local drop; no permits

spots.name: Kyllang Rock
spots.note: Bare granite dome above Mairang, twenty minutes up on foot; the rock stays cool in summer and the wind on top is fierce.

spots.name: Weinia Falls
spots.note: Falls off the Mairang to Shillong road with a path down to the pool; best after rain, the descent is slippery.

name: Mawphlang Sacred Forest
tagline: Khasi sacred grove where you may not carry a single leaf out

why.winter: Dec-Feb runs 4-16 C with frost on the grassland; the grove is dim and dripping but you will have it to yourself.
why.summer: March-April is the best walking window for the 16 km David Scott Trail down to Lad Mawphlang, before the rain.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug Khasi rain is relentless and the trail is a mudslide; by September it eases and the grove is deepest green.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is peak: clear skies over the grasslands, dry monoliths and the sacred forest at its most saturated green.

vibe: Village homestays and a heritage campsite, Khasi guides who explain the grove's taboos, silence after 4 pm
hub: Shillong 25 km, shared taxis from Bara Bazar about 1 h; Umroi airport 45 km; Guwahati 125 km

spots.name: David Scott Trail
spots.note: Sixteen km of the old British bridle path down to Lad Mawphlang; four to five hours, arrange the pickup before you start.

spots.name: Khasi Heritage Village
spots.note: Rebuilt Khasi houses and raised monoliths beside the grove, made for the Monolith Festival; same ticket counter.

spots.name: Lad Mawphlang
spots.note: Hamlet on the Umiew at the far end of the trail, with a swinging footbridge; shared taxis out dry up around 4 pm.

spots.name: Mawphlang Dam
spots.note: Quiet reservoir on the Umiew that supplies Shillong's water; an hour's walk on the banks, no boats and no shops.

name: Nongkhnum Island (Langshiang Falls)
tagline: Sand-beach river island above one of India's tallest falls

why.winter: Dec-Feb is dry and blue: the Kynshi shrinks to green pools, the sand flats double in size and island camping is at its safest.
why.summer: Mar-Apr stays warm and hazy but fine for the falls viewpoints; May's first storms make the river tracks greasy and slow.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the Kynshi runs in spate: the beach disappears, crossings are dangerous and the track from Nongstoin slides; stay away.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the sweet spot: Langshiang still thunders at near-monsoon volume while the sand beach re-emerges for tents.

vibe: Khasi herders and rare Shillong campers; sleep in a simple Nongstoin lodge or camp on the island with a local guide
hub: Shillong to Nongstoin 92 km by shared sumo, then 16 km of rough track; hire wheels locally; no permits

spots.name: Shadthum Falls
spots.note: The Phanliang branch of the Kynshi drops off the island's edge into a gorge; the rock at the lip stays wet, so keep back

spots.name: Weinia Falls
spots.note: The Namliang branch falls into a wooded gorge on the far side of the island, a short walk from the sand beach; loudest after rain

spots.name: Nongstoin
spots.note: The district town you come in through, with the nearest bank, market and hotel rooms; sumos for Shillong go by mid afternoon

name: Nongkhyllem Sanctuary (Lailad)
tagline: Elephant and hornbill forest on the Umtrew, off the Guwahati road

why.winter: Dec-Feb is prime: dry trails, no leeches, hornbills crossing the Umtrew and elephant sign on the fire lines, cold at first light
why.summer: March still walks well; April heats up and turns sticky, and May brings the first storms with the leeches back on the trails
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the forest roads wash out and the range office turns walkers back; September drips and the leeches own the paths
why.autumn: October is green and quiet after the rain, November is the birding month, clear mornings and easy boat runs on the river

vibe: A forest rest house and Lailad village rooms, a boatman on the water and a guide who knows the calls; evenings are properly dark
hub: Guwahati or Shillong to Nongpoh on NH6, then 12 km by hired jeep to Lailad; permit at the range office first

name: Nongriat (Double-Decker Root Bridge)
tagline: 3,500 steps down to a living double-decker root bridge

why.winter: Dry stone steps make the descent and climb back up far safer, cool weather helps.
why.summer: Air stays a mild 26C, but Sohra already takes 790 mm of rain in April and 1,300 mm in May, so the 3,500 steps get greasy early.
why.monsoon: Steps become a waterslide, genuinely dangerous plus leeches: most guesthouses say skip it.
why.autumn: Rainbow Falls swimming hole still full from monsoon, steps drying out nicely.

vibe: Riverside guesthouses full of trekkers, communal dinners, easy to find company.
hub: Drive to Tyrna (1h from Cherrapunji), trek 3,500 steps down. No ILP.

spots.name: Rainbow Falls
spots.note: An hour on past the root bridge, a hard climb to a blue plunge pool; go by 10 am for the rainbow in the spray

spots.name: Mawsaw Root Bridge
spots.note: Smaller living root bridge on the Rainbow Falls path with a clear pool under it, the best swim on the whole walk

spots.name: Ritymmen Root Bridge
spots.note: The long single decker root bridge at Nongthymmai, passed on the way down from Tyrna; most people walk straight past it

spots.name: Tyrna
spots.note: Trailhead village at the top of the 3,500 steps where taxis wait and porters are hired; the climb back up takes two hours

name: Ranikor (Kynshi river)
tagline: Green Kynshi river and white sand bars on the Bangladesh border

why.winter: Dec-Feb is the season: the river runs clear green, days sit near 25 C down in the valley, and anglers work the sand bars for mahseer
why.summer: March is still pleasant by the water; April and May push past 35 C in this low valley and pre-monsoon storms muddy the river
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the Kynshi is a brown flood, no boat goes out and the Mawkyrwat road slips; September drains slowly and stays humid
why.autumn: October clears the silt and the hills are green; November is dry, warm and empty, the best light on the gorge downstream

vibe: A border bazaar, a PWD bungalow and a few riverside rooms; evenings are anglers and fishermen, no cafes, lights out early
hub: Shared sumo from Shillong via Mawkyrwat, about 5 h of slow hill road; nothing leaves after early afternoon

name: Shillong
tagline: Northeast's hill capital: cafes, lakes, live music
festival: Nov: Shillong Cherry Blossom Festival

why.winter: Peak season: crisp clear days, misty mornings, easy walks around Ward's Lake without rain gear.
why.summer: Warm and pleasant before the rains hit, greener hills, noticeably fewer tourists than winter.
why.monsoon: City itself copes fine, but day trips to Cherrapunji get washed out and landslides can shut roads.
why.autumn: Best window: monsoon just ended, waterfalls still full, skies clearing fast, comfortable temps.

vibe: Cafe crowd and shared taxis. Easy to link up with travellers heading onward.
hub: Fly/bus to Guwahati, then 3h shared taxi to Shillong. No ILP.

spots.name: Iewduh (Bara Bazar)
spots.note: Khasi wholesale market spilling down the hillside, best before noon; carry a small bag and watch your pockets in the crush

spots.name: Laitlum Canyons
spots.note: Grass ridge dropping into a green gorge, 45 minutes out by taxi; cloud usually closes it in after 2 pm, so go early

spots.name: Don Bosco Centre for Indigenous Cultures
spots.note: Seven floors on the tribes of the northeast ending in a rooftop skywalk over the city; allow two hours, closed Sunday

spots.name: Ward's Lake
spots.note: Horseshoe lake with a wooden bridge and boats in the middle of town; nominal ticket, open till dusk, good for an hour

spots.name: Umiam Lake
spots.note: Big reservoir on the Guwahati road, viewpoint above the dam and kayaks at the water sports complex; best at sunset

spots.name: Elephant Falls
spots.note: Three tier fall down concrete steps, busy with tour buses; small ticket, ten minutes down and back, thin water in spring

spots.name: Dylan's Cafe
spots.note: Bob Dylan themed cafe in Laitumkhrah with coffee, cake and a guitar in the corner; one small room, expect to share a table

spots.name: Shillong Peak
spots.note: The highest point over the city, inside an air force area; carry photo ID and check it is open, it shuts without notice

name: Siju (Dobakkol Caves)
tagline: Limestone bat caves and a bird sanctuary on the Simsang river

why.winter: Nov-Feb is the only safe caving window: the Simsang is low, the passages are wadeable and the air sits at 12-26 C.
why.summer: March-May turns humid and 35 C at this low altitude, and pre-monsoon storms can put water into the cave fast.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the Simsang rises into the cave mouths, the road south of Tura slides and caving is off the table.
why.autumn: October drains slowly and the river drops enough to enter by late month, with the sanctuary at its greenest.

vibe: One basic lodge and a forest rest house; you hire a village guide with a torch and meet no other visitors
hub: Shared Sumo from Tura 2.5 h on the Baghmara road; bring your own torch and cash, facilities are minimal

spots.name: Siju Wildlife Sanctuary
spots.note: Wetland and forest on the Simsang beside the caves, known for hornbills and winter ducks; take a village guide, no marked trails

spots.name: Simsang River
spots.note: The green river the cave mouth opens onto; villagers will paddle you along the cliffs for a small fee, lowest in winter

name: Tura (Garo Hills)
tagline: Garo hills base for Nokrek, Siju caves and a hundred drums
festival: Nov: 100 Drums Wangala at Asanang (dates shift yearly)

why.winter: Dec-Feb stays dry at 10-26 C and still works for the Nokrek trail and the long road south to Balpakram.
why.summer: March-April is hot at this low altitude and hazy with jhum burning; May brings the first Garo hills downpours.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the Garo hills take huge rain and the Williamnagar and Baghmara roads slide, so travel becomes guesswork.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the payoff: harvest under way, the 100 Drums Wangala at Asanang 18 km out, and clear ridge air.

vibe: Garo town with basic hotels and no traveller circuit; you will be the only outsider on most shared jeeps
hub: Guwahati 220 km by bus, 6-7 h via Goalpara; Baljek airport near Tura is built but not operational

spots.name: Tura Peak
spots.note: Wooded hill straight above town, about two hours up to the observatory and back; start by 7 am, it clouds in later

spots.name: Nokrek National Park
spots.note: Biosphere forest around the highest peak of the Garo hills, with wild citrus groves; permit and guide from the Tura forest office

spots.name: Pelga Falls
spots.note: Wide falls on the Ganol river where Tura families picnic on Sundays; shallow enough to wade, come midweek for it empty

spots.name: Asanang
spots.note: Ground where the Hundred Drums Wangala is danced every November; outside the festival week it is a quiet Garo village

spots.name: Tura Bazar
spots.note: Town market for Garo produce, dried fish and jackfruit; busiest on weekend mornings and the last place to stock up for Nokrek

name: Wahkhen (Mawryngkhang Bamboo Trail)
tagline: Bamboo skywalk over the Wahrew gorge to the king of stones

why.winter: Dec-Feb is dry-season safe on the lashed bamboo spans, cool in the gorge, and clear enough to watch the Wahrew far below your feet.
why.summer: Mar-Apr works with an early start before haze fills the gorge; carry water, the 3-4 h round trip has none along the way.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug is a no: rain makes the bamboo walkways lethal over the drops and the Wahrew floods; wait for the dry-season repairs.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is prime: freshly rebuilt walkways, a full river under your feet and the rock towers at their photogenic best.

vibe: Village guides and Shillong day-trekkers, quiet midweek; most sleep back in Shillong, Wahkhen keeps a homestay or two
hub: 55 km from Shillong via Pomlum; taxi day-hire is the practical way in; Umroi airport 75 km; no permits

spots.name: Wahrew River
spots.note: The gorge the bamboo walkway hangs over; the pools at the bottom of the trail are good to sit in, and rise fast in rain

spots.name: Nongjrong
spots.note: Cliff village over the Bangladesh plains, known for a sea of cloud at sunrise; you have to leave Wahkhen by about 4 am

spots.name: Mawkynrew
spots.note: Block town on the road in from Shillong and the last shops and tea before the trailhead; taxis for Wahkhen turn off here

name: Wari Chora (Emangre)
tagline: Slot canyon of still green water, rafted from Emangre village
festival: Nov: Wangala drums in the Garo villages

why.winter: Dec-Feb is when the gorge works: low clear water, bamboo rafts running, warm days and cold nights in the Emangre homestays
why.summer: March is fine and hot; by April and May a storm upriver can raise the canyon within an hour and the guides call the rafts off
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the gorge floods brown and the Emangre track turns to clay: the village closes the trip, do not try to talk your way in
why.autumn: October water is still high and silty, so leave it to the end of the month; November is clear, green and almost nobody else

vibe: Village homestays with bucket baths, a community guide fee and dinner of rice and pork; no phone signal down at the water
hub: Sumo Guwahati to Baghmara (9 h), jeep to Emangre, then a guided walk down to the raft point, no entry on your own

name: Aizawl
tagline: Mizoram's hillside capital: churches, cafes, rock music
festival: Early Mar: Chapchar Kut spring festival

why.winter: Best weather: cool, dry, clear views across the hill ridges the city is built on.
why.summer: Warm and pleasant into April, then humidity builds fast as the rains approach.
why.monsoon: Sits in one of India's wettest monsoon belts. Daily downpours, occasional landslides.
why.autumn: October skies clear up nicely, a good shoulder window with fewer visitors.

vibe: Church-going, coffee-shop city: safe and welcoming, small traveller scene.
hub: Fly to Lengpui airport, 40min out. ILP + PAP.

spots.name: Bara Bazar
spots.note: Stacked hillside market where Mizo women sell herbs, bamboo shoot and dried fish; go in the morning, the city shuts Sunday

spots.name: Solomon's Temple
spots.note: Enormous white church on the western edge of the city, built by a local congregation; open to visitors by day, dress neatly

spots.name: Mizoram State Museum
spots.note: Small state collection of Mizo dress, weapons and village life; an hour is plenty, and it is closed on Sundays

spots.name: KV Paradise
spots.note: Marble mausoleum a man built at Durtlang for his wife, her car and clothes inside; small ticket, wide view over Aizawl

name: Champhai (Murlen & Vangchhia)
tagline: Mizoram's rice-bowl valley of vineyards on the Myanmar rim

why.winter: Nov-Feb is the window: dry 8-20 C days, the paddy chequerboard sharp below town and clear runs out to the Vangchhia menhirs.
why.summer: Mar-Apr is warm with jhum-burning haze on the hills; still fine for Murlen forest walks before the rain arrives.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug rains hard and the hill cuttings between Aizawl and Champhai slip; the valley hides in cloud for days.
why.autumn: October is freshly rinsed and quiet: harvest in the rice bowl, orchids in Murlen and the menhir field to yourself.

vibe: A relaxed border town of church spires, simple hotels and local grape wine; travellers are rare and locals chat easily
hub: ILP for non-Mizoram Indians; Aizawl to Champhai 190 km, 7-8 h by shared sumo; Murlen NP is 45 km further

spots.name: Hnahlan
spots.note: Grape growing village north of Champhai where the small wineries press; ask around and someone will show you a cellar

spots.name: Rih Dil
spots.note: Heart shaped lake a few km inside Myanmar, sacred in Mizo belief; the Zokhawthar crossing is restricted now, ask at the post

spots.name: Zokhawthar
spots.note: Border village on the Tiau river where the bridge to Myanmar stands; go in the morning and check the rules at the border post

name: Dampa Tiger Reserve (Teirei)
tagline: Clouded-leopard rainforest on the Bangladesh border, explored only on foot

why.winter: Dec-Feb is the dry window: cool mornings at the Teirei rest house, guided walks to salt licks and watchtowers, gibbons calling at dawn. Book through the Field Director.
why.summer: March is still good on the trails; April brings jhum-burning haze and heat at 260 m, May pre-monsoon storms and the first leeches, so go early in the season.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the reserve is shut: 2,000 mm of rain washes out the West Phaileng-Teirei track and the forest trails, and the rest house does not take visitors. Not now.
why.autumn: October reopens the gates with the forest at its greenest and streams still full; November dries the paths and is the best month for birds and gibbons.

vibe: A 30-house hamlet and a forest rest house with dorm beds at Rs 150, rice-and-dal dinner at 6 pm, then a black sky and cicadas
hub: Aizawl to West Phaileng 100 km (4 h by car or sumo), 14 km more to Teirei; permit from the Chief Wildlife Warden, Aizawl

name: Hmuifang
tagline: Protected chiefs' forest ridge at 1,500 m south of Aizawl

why.winter: Nov-Feb is the reason to come: 5-18 C, dry air, and a 45 minute climb to a summit view over half of Mizoram.
why.summer: March-April stays walkable but jhum burning smokes out the view, and May turns muggy as the first rains arrive.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the ridge sits in cloud for days, leeches own the forest trail and the Thenzawl road slips regularly.
why.autumn: October clears fast after the rains and the lodge is near empty; nights already need a fleece at 1,500 m.

vibe: A state tourism lodge and a few village homestays; Aizawl families at weekends and no other travellers
hub: Shared Sumo from Aizawl 1.5 h on the Thenzawl road; Lengpui airport 85 km; ILP for non-Mizoram Indians

spots.name: Hmuifang Tlang
spots.note: Forty minutes up through the old chiefs' forest to the ridge top; go at first light, the cloud sea burns off by nine

spots.name: Sialsuk
spots.note: The nearest proper village, down the Thenzawl road, with shops and a place to eat; shared sumos stop here both ways

name: Palak Dil (Phura)
tagline: Mizoram's largest lake, a forest walk from a Mara village near the Myanmar border

why.winter: Nov-Feb the 6 km trail from Phura is dry and leech-free, the lake sits glassy under mist till 9 am and winter ducks join the 200-plus bird list; nights a mild 10-12 C.
why.summer: March and April stay walkable but hot and hazy, 32 C by noon with jhum smoke over the hills; by May thunderstorms hit most afternoons and the lake path turns to mud.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug southern Mizoram takes 3,000 mm of rain: the Siaha-Phura road slips, sumos stop for days and the trail is a leech bath. September eases off and the lake is brim full.
why.autumn: October clears with the forest at its greenest and the lake at its widest; November is the sweet spot, dry trails, clear skies, and most days the whole shore is yours.

vibe: A Mara village of tin roofs and a church bell, a government tourist lodge and a bamboo forest lodge; evenings are early and quiet
hub: Night sumo Aizawl to Siaha, 378 km (12 h), then a daily sumo to Phura (3 h); the lake is a 6 km forest walk from there

name: Phawngpui (Blue Mountain)
tagline: Mizoram's highest ridge, a grass bowl above nesting falcons

why.winter: Nov-Mar is dry at 5-20 C on top, and the Farpak meadow walk and the Thlazuang Kham cliff edge are straightforward.
why.summer: Rhododendron and orchids peak in March-April, but from May the Sangau road turns to clay and the summit clouds in.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the park is shut outright: permits are issued only from November to end-April, and the Sangau road slips under the rain anyway.
why.autumn: October is still outside the permit window: the park only reopens in November, so the summit and Farpak are off-limits.

vibe: You sleep in Sangau village homestays and walk up with a forest guard, expecting no other trekkers at all
hub: ILP for Indians; Aizawl to Sangau 230 km, 9-10 h by shared sumo, then a hired jeep to the park gate

spots.name: Farpak
spots.note: Grass meadow below the summit where the trail comes out, orchids and rhododendron in March; the park camp sits here

spots.name: Thlazuang Kham
spots.note: Sheer cliff on the far side of the summit bowl where falcons nest; the drop is unfenced, keep well back in wind

spots.name: Sangau
spots.note: Base village with the homestays and the forest office; fix the park permit and a guide here, there is nothing up top

name: Reiek
tagline: Ridge-top village with hiking trails and border views

why.winter: Clearest ridge views, cool hiking weather, best season to see the peak's rock formations.
why.summer: Pleasant into April, green hillsides, then humidity builds toward the rains.
why.monsoon: Same wet Mizoram monsoon belt as Aizawl. Trails turn slick, views vanish into cloud.
why.autumn: Cloud lifts through October and the Bangladesh plains come back into view from 1,465 m; nights turn cool and the heritage village empties.

vibe: Half-day escape from Aizawl: cultural-village shows, mostly domestic day-trippers.
hub: 1h drive from Aizawl. ILP + PAP for foreigners.

spots.name: Reiek Tlang
spots.note: Steep forty minute climb through forest to the rock summit looking out at the Bangladesh plains; slippery when wet

spots.name: Mizo Heritage Village
spots.note: Replica village of thatched chiefs' houses at the foot of the hill; small ticket, and it fills up for the Anthurium Festival

spots.name: Tuirihiau Falls
spots.note: Fall you can walk in behind, down a rough path below the village; the return climb is steep, skip it alone after rain

name: Tamdil Lake (Saitual)
tagline: Forest-rimmed lake at 780 m near Saitual, with a lakeside lodge and kayaks

why.winter: Dec-Feb the lake sits under a dawn mist that burns off by 9, days run 8-20 C and the lodge is mostly empty on weekdays; Aizawl families fill the picnic sheds on Saturdays.
why.summer: March is cool and clear enough for the forest trails; April and May turn hazy and humid, though at 780 m the lake stays cooler than Aizawl and the boats still run.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the hills are their greenest and the lake brims, but 2,000 mm of rain means boats stop in downpours and forest paths are leechy; the Saitual road stays open.
why.autumn: October's washed skies make it the best month for kayaking and forest walks; November evenings turn cold at the lodge, so carry a layer for the lakeside verandah.

vibe: Weekend picnic families from Aizawl by day, a near-empty Tourism Dept lodge by night; evenings are a lakeside walk and an early dinner
hub: Aizawl to Saitual about 100 km by sumo (3 h, Mon-Sat), then 6 km by taxi to the lake; Lengpui airport is 30 km beyond Aizawl

name: Thenzawl (Vantawng Falls)
tagline: Mizoram's tallest fall and a handloom town in the Serchhip hills

why.winter: Dec-Feb is dry and easy in the weaving sheds, but Vantawng thins to two white threads down its 200 m cliff.
why.summer: March-April is hazy with jhum smoke and the fall is at its weakest; from May the Aizawl road starts washing out.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the fall is huge and useless at once, because the gorge fills with cloud and the viewing tower sees nothing.
why.autumn: October is the month it lines up: full post-monsoon flow, clear gorge air and the deer park green after the rain.

vibe: Weaver-run guesthouses and a state lodge; day visitors from Aizawl at the tower, no traveller scene at all
hub: Shared Sumo from Aizawl, 85 km and 3 h; fall viewing tower 5 km on; ILP for non-Mizoram Indians

spots.name: Chawngchilhi Puk
spots.note: Cliff cave tied to the Mizo legend of the girl and the serpent; take a torch and a local pointer, the path is unmarked

spots.name: Thenzawl Golf Resort
spots.note: A full course cut into the hills outside town and rarely busy; day green fees and club hire at the clubhouse desk

spots.name: Thenzawl Deer Park
spots.note: Forest department enclosure of sambar and barking deer in a wooded valley; early morning is the only time they are out

spots.name: Serchhip
spots.note: District town up the road with the nearest bank, pharmacy and sumo counters for Aizawl; useful rather than worth a look

name: Benreu (Mount Pauna)
tagline: Zeliang village at 1,900 m under Mount Pauna, a moss-forest climb with Barail views
festival: mid Feb: Hega, the Zeliang festival

why.winter: Dec-Feb are dry and sharp: frost on the terraces some mornings, clean sightlines from the Pauna summit to the Barail range and Assam plains; Hega fills the village mid Feb.
why.summer: March is still clear and cool for the 2-3 h climb; by April the plains haze creeps up and afternoon storms begin, though the moss forest is greenest and orchids are out.
why.monsoon: Jul-Aug the Peren road slides and the summit trail turns to leech-ridden mud, so sit it out. June and September are wet but walkable, with waterfalls on the village slopes.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov after the rains the forest drips, paddy on the terraces is being cut and the summit gives its first clean views of the year; the cottages are rarely full.

vibe: Wooden cottages run by the Zeliang village council plus a few homestays; evenings are a fire, rice beer if you ask, and total dark.
hub: Dimapur air/rail, 3h by shared Sumo to Peren via Jalukie, then a hired jeep 20 km up to Benreu; Kohima about 3h; ILP needed

name: Doyang Reservoir (Pangti)
tagline: A million Amur falcons roost here each Oct-Nov, guarded by villagers who hunted them
festival: early Nov: Amur Falcon Festival at Pangti

why.winter: Dec-Feb the falcons are long gone (they leave by late November); what is left is a still reservoir under morning mist, some winter waterfowl and quiet Lotha villages.
why.summer: Mar-May the dam level drops and the reservoir shore at 300 m turns hot and hazy; Pangti's ridge at 1,000 m stays cooler, but there is little reason to come before the birds.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the Wokha hill roads slide and the reservoir sits under rain, so skip it. September is still wet, and the first falcons only appear around the middle of October.
why.autumn: Mid Oct to mid Nov is the whole point: up to a million falcons lift off the roost at first light and pour back at dusk. Be at the tower by 4.30 am; book a homestay ahead.

vibe: Lotha homestays in Pangti or the NEEPCO guest house at the dam; birders, a few photographers and guides who walk you out at 4 am.
hub: Dimapur air/rail to Wokha by shared Sumo (4h), then a hired jeep 30 km to Pangti (1.5h); Kohima to Wokha is 3h; ILP needed

name: Dzukou Valley
tagline: Rolling green trekking valley famous for summer lilies

why.winter: Cold and frost-covered, grass turns brown, but skies stay clear: pack warm layers.
why.summer: Dry-season trekking, brown rather than green, but trails are safe and views are clear.
why.monsoon: The famous Dzukou lilies bloom in June-July, but you'll fight mud, leeches and fog for it.
why.autumn: The sweet spot: late blooms linger, then the valley turns lush green with the clearest views.

vibe: Trekking-hut camaraderie: shared meals cooked over a wood stove with fellow hikers.
hub: From Kohima: 1h drive + 3-4h trek from Viswema. ILP covers it.

spots.name: Viswema
spots.note: Southern Angami village where the gentler trail starts; shared taxis from Kohima drop you at the road head by 9 am.

spots.name: Jakhama
spots.note: The other trail head, steeper and shorter at about 3 h up; taxis from Kohima take 40 minutes to the village.

spots.name: Japfu Peak
spots.note: At 3048 m the state's second summit, a steep climb from Jakhama; the haze clears at sunrise, so start before dawn.

spots.name: Dzukou River
spots.note: The icy stream threading the valley floor under the boulders; it is the only water source, so fill up before you climb out.

name: Khonoma
tagline: Angami stone village that banned hunting and kept its terraces
festival: Feb: Sekrenyi (Angami purification, 25 Feb)

why.winter: Nov-Feb is clear at 4-18 C, the alder terraces are bare gold and Sekrenyi in late February is the village at full tilt.
why.summer: March-April is warm with rhododendron on the tragopan sanctuary ridge before the pre-monsoon cloud closes in.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the Kohima road slips, and the terraces look wonderful while the trails are leech-covered and always wet.
why.autumn: October is green and quiet, a far calmer base than Kohima in the build-up to the December Hornbill festival crush.

vibe: Angami homestays with wood fires and rice beer, guided walks, and a fort ridge you climb before breakfast
hub: ILP for Indians; Kohima 20 km, shared taxis about 1 h; Dimapur airport and railhead 90 km, 3 h

spots.name: Khonoma Fort
spots.note: Stone gate and ramparts the Angami held against the British in 1879; ten minutes uphill from the village square.

spots.name: Khonoma Tragopan Sanctuary
spots.note: Community forest the village set aside after banning hunting in 1998; Blyth's tragopan is shy, take a village guide.

spots.name: Khonoma Rice Terraces
spots.note: Alder fed terraces stacked down the whole valley below the village; best light in the hour after sunrise, greenest in July.

spots.name: Dzuleke
spots.note: Tiny valley hamlet an hour past Khonoma with a trout stream and a few homestays; the road is rough, hire a taxi in Kohima.

spots.name: Khonoma Baptist Church
spots.note: White church on the ridge that is now the centre of village life; the Angami service on Sunday morning fills it by 9 am.

name: Kohima
tagline: Naga hill capital and gateway to Hornbill Festival
festival: Dec 1-10: Hornbill Festival, Kisama Village

why.winter: December is peak: Hornbill Festival packs Kisama; January-February stay cool and clear too.
why.summer: Pleasant hill-station warmth through May, comfortable temperatures, fewer crowds than festival time.
why.monsoon: Heavy rain on steep hill roads brings regular landslides around the district.
why.autumn: October-November is lovely, clear skies building toward December's festival crowds.

vibe: Hornbill month is a huge friendly crowd; otherwise a quiet WWII-history town.
hub: Fly Dimapur, 3h shared taxi to Kohima. ILP + PAP.

spots.name: Kohima War Cemetery
spots.note: Terraced graves on Garrison Hill from the 1944 battle, with the tennis court line marked in stone; free, sunrise to sunset.

spots.name: Naga Heritage Village, Kisama
spots.note: A morung for every Naga tribe on one hillside and the Hornbill Festival ground each December; quiet and cheap the rest of the year.

spots.name: Kohima Cathedral
spots.note: Naga roofed cathedral on Aradura Hill built with Japanese help after the 1944 battle; climb up for the view over the town.

spots.name: Nagaland State Museum
spots.note: Tribe by tribe display of shawls, log drums and headgear at Bayavu Hill; closed Sundays, an hour is enough.

spots.name: Mao Market
spots.note: Naga produce market running to bamboo shoot, axone, herbs and river fish; go before 10 am, it thins out by afternoon.

spots.name: WWII Museum, Kisama
spots.note: The 1944 battle told through recovered weapons, letters and a relief map; it sits beside the heritage village, so pair the two.

name: Longwa (Mon district)
tagline: Konyak village whose chief's house sits astride the frontier
festival: Apr: Aoleang Monyu (Konyak new year, 1-6 Apr)

why.winter: Nov-Feb is dry at 6-20 C, the Mon road is passable, fog sits below the village and the hearth fires stay lit.
why.summer: Aoleang in the first week of April is the year's big draw, and by late May the hill road starts breaking up again.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the Mon-Longwa road is deep mud, and the last 40 km can take five hours or simply not happen that day.
why.autumn: October dries week by week and roads improve, but the ride up from Mon stays rough and hard to time reliably.

vibe: Konyak homestays and a village guesthouse, tattooed elders, and no traveller scene outside festival week
hub: ILP for Indians; Mon town 42 km on broken road, 2-3 h; Sonari railhead 90 km; Jorhat airport 200 km

spots.name: Longwa Angh's House
spots.note: The Konyak chief's longhouse straddles the border, kitchen in India and bed in Myanmar; ask before you enter or photograph.

spots.name: Veda Peak
spots.note: High point above the Mon hills with ridges running into Myanmar on both sides; a rough jeep hour, then a short climb up.

spots.name: Shangnyu
spots.note: Konyak village with a big carved wooden monument in the Angh's compound; ask in Mon whether the road is passable in rain.

name: Mokokchung
tagline: Ao Naga heartland of ridge villages and Moatsu drumming
festival: May: Moatsu (Ao festival, 1-3 May)

why.winter: Nov-Mar is dry at 8-22 C, good for walking out to Longkhum and Ungma and for the long ridge views over Assam.
why.summer: Moatsu in the first days of May is the reason to come in summer; otherwise April is warm, hazy and very quiet.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the ridge roads from Amguri slide, shared sumos cancel and the views vanish into more or less constant cloud.
why.autumn: October is clean and green with the harvest under way, and the town's plain hotels are cheap and nearly empty.

vibe: Ridge-top college town, Baptist Sunday quiet, plain hotels, and Ao villages you reach by shared sumo
hub: ILP for Indians; Dimapur airport and railhead 160 km, 5 h; Jorhat 105 km via Amguri, 4 h by sumo

spots.name: Ungma
spots.note: The oldest and largest Ao village and seat of its chiefs; walk up for the morung carvings and the view back over town.

spots.name: Longkhum
spots.note: Ridge village where Ao spirits are said to rest before leaving; people come for the sunset over the plains, so stay the night.

spots.name: Mopungchuket
spots.note: Model Ao village with a landscaped park, a museum hut and the Jina and Etiben story; small entry ticket, best on a dry day.

spots.name: Chuchuyimlang
spots.note: Village known for Moatsu in the first week of May, when the log drum and rice beer come out; little to see off season.

spots.name: Langpangkong Caves
spots.note: Caves in the Langpangkong ridge where an Ahom king is said to have hidden; slippery steps, carry a torch and take a guide.

name: Pfutsero (Glory Peak)
tagline: Nagaland's highest and coldest town, cherry-blossom lanes under Glory Peak
festival: mid Jan: Sukrunye, the Chakhesang purification festival

why.winter: Dec-Feb nights drop below freezing and the Glory Peak dawn opens clean sightlines over the Chakhesang hills; Sukrunye on 15 Jan fills the town. Carry a real jacket.
why.summer: March is crisp and clear; April warms and the plains haze softens the views, while wild orchids and the kiwi and persimmon orchards flower around Chizami and Khezhakeno.
why.monsoon: June rain sets in hard and Jul-Aug bring landslides on the Kohima hill road and fog on the ridge; September is still wet but the terraces glow before harvest.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is peak: harvest on the Khezhakeno and Chizami terraces, then mid-November's wild cherry blossom turns the town lanes pink for about two weeks.

vibe: A government tourist lodge and plain guesthouses; Chizami weavers' cooperatives, church bells at dawn, tea shops and an early bedtime.
hub: Kohima to Pfutsero is 70 km of hill road, 2.5-3h by shared Sumo; Dimapur airport and railhead are 5-6h by Sumo; ILP needed

name: Shilloi Lake (Latsam)
tagline: Foot-shaped sacred lake below Phek's pine ridges near Myanmar

why.winter: Dec-Feb is still and blue with near-frost nights; mist burns off the water by 8 am and you may not meet another visitor all day.
why.summer: March is fine and quiet; Apr-May greens the ridges but afternoon storms make the long Phek roads slow and greasy.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the day-long approach from Kohima crawls with slips and fog while the lake sulks in grey; not worth the grind.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is best: post-rain clarity, terraced paddy gold around Lutsam village and calm water at the lakeside huts.

vibe: A small government tourist cottage by the shore and Lutsam homestays; locals hold the water sacred, so nights are hushed
hub: ILP online; from Kohima a full day via Pfutsero and Phek, 8-9 h; hire a taxi in Phek, sumos are scarce

spots.name: Meluri
spots.note: Pochury town and the road head for the lake, with the last shops, fuel and phone signal; sumos from Kohima terminate here.

spots.name: Phek
spots.note: Ridge top district town of terraced fields and a Saturday market; hire a taxi here, shared vehicles to the lake are rare.

name: Thanamir (Mount Saramati)
tagline: Yimkhiung apple village at 2,000 m, base camp for 3,826 m Mount Saramati

why.winter: Dec-Feb are the clearest months for the two-day summit push: frost at the ridge camp, the odd snowfall on top, Myanmar's ranges in sight at dawn. Carry a proper sleeping bag.
why.summer: March brings rhododendron on the upper trail and April is still dry enough for the climb; by May pre-monsoon storms roll in every afternoon and the summit hides in cloud.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the Kiphire and Pungro roads slide, the trail vanishes under undergrowth and leeches, and the peak stays in cloud. September's rain eases as the apples ripen.
why.autumn: October dries the trail while the last apples are still on the trees; November is the sweet spot, cold clear nights, no cloud on the summit and the village guides are free.

vibe: Village council homestays with wood-fire kitchens and apple orchards; a few trekkers a week in season, nights silent and cold.
hub: Dimapur air/rail to Kiphire by shared Sumo (10-12h via Kohima), Kiphire to Pungro 2h, then 20 km of rough road; ILP needed

name: Touphema Village
tagline: Angami hilltop village where you sleep in traditional huts
festival: Feb: Sekrenyi celebrated in the village (late Feb)

why.winter: Dec-Feb is cold and clear at 3-18 C: morung-style huts, kitchen fires, rice beer and Sekrenyi feasting in late February.
why.summer: Mar-Apr is mild with blossom on the terraces below the hill; May turns humid as the first hard showers arrive.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the hut verandas stare into fog while side roads off the Wokha highway chew up; damp, empty, skip it.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is harvest gold on the terraces and the run-up to Hornbill; book ahead, December overflow fills the huts.

vibe: Community-run huts with home food and rice beer; a handful of guests, mostly Hornbill-season overflow from Kohima
hub: ILP online; Dimapur airport-railhead to Kohima 3 h, then 41 km north on the Wokha road, about 1.5 h more

spots.name: Tseminyu
spots.note: Rengma district town further up the road north, with a roadside market and terraced fields; the only real stop that way.

name: Belghar (Kandhamal)
tagline: Sal-forest plateau of Kondh hamlets and elephant tracks

why.winter: Dec-Jan falls to 6 C at night on the plateau and the camp runs a wood fire; days are clear and elephant tracks show on the forest roads.
why.summer: Mar-May the sal drops its leaves and the streams shrink to pools; 36 C by afternoon, but 700 m keeps the nights cool and the walking easy.
why.monsoon: Jul-Aug the ghat road from Balliguda slips and the forest camp usually shuts; June and late September are the safer edges of the rains.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the green window, streams still running, mist off the plateau at dawn and the road patched up again. Book the camp ahead.

vibe: Forest tents and a village homestay or two, patchy phone signal; evenings are a wood fire and whatever the kitchen cooked
hub: Bus or shared jeep from Balliguda, about 45 km of ghat road; nearest railhead Muniguda, roughly 60 km

name: Bhitarkanika National Park
tagline: Mangrove creeks packed with 6 m saltwater crocodiles

why.winter: Dec-Feb is prime: crocodiles bask on every mudbank and waders crowd the creeks, bar a short census closure.
why.summer: The park shuts 1 May to 31 Jul for crocodile breeding, and April before that is 37 C and airless on a boat.
why.monsoon: Closed until 31 July; August and September reopen wet, with swollen creeks and boatmen who cancel often.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov works once the rain stops, but a Bay of Bengal cyclone can shut the jetties at a day's notice.

vibe: Forest rest houses at Dangmal and eco-camps near Khola; you share the boat with birders, not backpackers
hub: Bhadrak railhead 90 km, bus to Rajnagar, then a boat from Khola or Gupti; book the forest permit online

spots.name: Dangmal Crocodile Centre
spots.note: Pens and a small museum by the forest rest house where the saltwater crocodile programme began in 1975; walk it before the boat.

spots.name: Bagagahana Heronry
spots.note: Open water rookery where egrets, storks and darters nest through the monsoon months; boat only, and the morning light is better.

spots.name: Habalikhati Beach
spots.note: Casuarina backed sand at the Gahirmatha edge where olive ridleys nest; long boat ride, forest permit, and no shops at all.

spots.name: Khola Jetty
spots.note: The creek side entry point from the Rajnagar road where boats are hired; check the tide, low water can strand you for hours.

name: Bhubaneswar
tagline: Temple city of 700 shrines plus the Khandagiri Jain caves
festival: Jan: Adivasi Mela tribal fair

why.winter: Dec-Feb is the window: 15-28 C, dry mornings at Lingaraj and the Khandagiri caves, Adivasi Mela in January.
why.summer: Apr-May hits 42 C with sticky coastal air; the sandstone temples radiate heat and you give up by 10 am.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep is muggy and wet in bursts, but the temples, caves and state museum stay open and rooms get cheap.
why.autumn: October dries out fast and November is near-perfect, though a Bay of Bengal cyclone can still eat a week.

vibe: Government-town calm with a real hostel scene near KIIT, cheap autos, and pilgrims rather than backpackers
hub: Biju Patnaik airport and Bhubaneswar junction are in the city; Puri and Konark are 1-2 h by bus

spots.name: Lingaraj Temple
spots.note: The 11th century Shiva temple that anchors the old town and is still working; non Hindus see it from the viewing platform.

spots.name: Udayagiri and Khandagiri Caves
spots.note: Jain monk cells cut into two facing hills before the Christian era, with the Hathigumpha inscription; go early, the rock heats up.

spots.name: Mukteshwar Temple
spots.note: Small 10th century temple with a carved torana arch, the finest stone work in the city; free, and quiet before the tour buses.

spots.name: Dhauli Shanti Stupa
spots.note: Ashoka's rock edict and a white peace pagoda above the Daya river where the Kalinga war ended; best at sunset, autos wait below.

spots.name: Nandankanan Zoological Park
spots.note: Zoo and lion safari in sal forest with white tigers and a lake boat; closed Mondays, and a half day once you add the queue.

spots.name: Museum of Tribal Arts and Artefacts
spots.note: Full scale huts of Odisha's tribes with their tools, ornaments and drums, near CRP Square; free entry, allow an hour.

name: Chandipur (Balasore)
tagline: The sea walks out up to 5 km at low tide and returns

why.winter: Dec-Feb is the season: 12-27 C, a firm exposed seabed to walk at low tide and red crabs everywhere.
why.summer: April-May is 40 C on an unshaded flat and pre-monsoon squalls off the Bay start turning the sea ugly.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the tidal flat is a grey soup, the shacks shut and the whole vanishing-sea trick is lost.
why.autumn: October is cyclone month on this coast; from mid-November the light is clean and the crowds are thin.

vibe: A quiet retiree-and-family beach with an OTDC Panthanivas and small hotels; walk the seabed at dawn
hub: Balasore railhead is 16 km with autos all day; the beach shuts for DRDO missile tests now and then

spots.name: Balaramgadi
spots.note: Fishing harbour where the Budhabalanga meets the sea; the boats come in around dawn and the catch is auctioned on the sand.

spots.name: Kshira Chora Gopinath Temple
spots.note: Remuna's Vaishnav temple known for the stolen kheer story; the kheer bhog is still given out, and morning arati is the time.

spots.name: Panchalingeswar Temple
spots.note: Five lingas lying under a hill stream on Nilagiri, up a long flight of steps; you feel for them underwater, go on a weekday.

spots.name: Kuldiha Wildlife Sanctuary
spots.note: Sal forest with elephants and hornbills, entered from Nilagiri; you need a jeep and a forest permit, there are no walk ins.

name: Chandragiri (Jirang Tibetan Settlement)
tagline: Tibetan refugee camps and a gold-roofed monastery in the Gajapati hills
festival: Feb/Mar: Losar at the Phuntsokling settlement

why.winter: Dec-Feb is cool and clear at 600 m with mist in the valley at dawn, and Losar in February or March fills the monastery courtyard.
why.summer: March is comfortable. April and May push 38 C in the valley, though evenings cool off and the monastery hall stays shaded all day.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the Gajapati ridges go green and cloud sits on them; the Mohana road gets patchy and leeches come out, but the camps are quiet.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov brings the best light of the year here, clear ridges, cut paddy below and 28 C days for walking between the settlement camps.

vibe: A 1963 refugee settlement of low houses and prayer flags, a monastery guest house and momo kitchens; nothing open after 8 pm
hub: Bus from Brahmapur, about 90 km, or from Paralakhemundi via Mohana; Brahmapur is also the nearest railhead

name: Chilika Lake (Satapada)
tagline: Asia's largest lagoon: dolphins and migratory birds

why.winter: The only season worth the trip. Dolphins more active, Nalabana fills with migratory birds.
why.summer: Water levels drop and heat makes open boat rides uncomfortable; dolphin sightings get harder.
why.monsoon: Freshwater inflow clouds the lagoon and rough water makes dolphin boats unreliable.
why.autumn: Oct is a quieter early option; birds and dolphins are still building toward the winter peak.

vibe: Day-trip crowd from Puri - sharing a dolphin boat is the easiest way to meet people.
hub: 1.5hr drive from Puri to Satapada jetty for boat tours.

spots.name: Rajhans Island
spots.note: Sand spit where the lagoon opens to the sea, the far point of the dolphin boat; two hours there and back, no shade or food.

spots.name: Nalabana Bird Sanctuary
spots.note: Reed island that fills with migratory birds from December to February; needs a forest permit, an early boat and binoculars.

spots.name: Alarnath Temple
spots.note: Brahmagiri's Vishnu temple where Puri pilgrims go while Jagannath is in seclusion; packed in the Anasara fortnight of June.

name: Daringbadi
tagline: 'Kashmir of Odisha': pine forests, frost, coffee gardens

why.winter: The whole reason to come. Frost most mornings, occasional snow, genuinely cold for Odisha.
why.summer: Cooler than the plains but still warm by midday; waterfalls run thin until the rains arrive.
why.monsoon: Waterfalls run full and the forest turns lush, but ghat roads get landslide-prone and slick.
why.autumn: Pleasant and green post-monsoon, with the first hints of winter chill by late November.

vibe: Barely any tourist infrastructure - mostly Kandha villagers, not backpackers.
hub: 7hr drive from Bhubaneswar via Phulbani; own vehicle recommended.

spots.name: Hill View Park
spots.note: The town's own ridge park looking over pine and coffee slopes; small ticket, and the valley mist burns off by about 9 am.

spots.name: Midubanda Waterfall
spots.note: Forest fall on the Belghar road with a short walk down to the pool; strongest just after the rains, a trickle by March.

spots.name: Doluri River
spots.note: Shallow rocky river where local families picnic on the sand; shared autos run out from town, and there is no food stall.

spots.name: Daringbadi Coffee Plantation
spots.note: The coffee and pepper slopes that made this hill famous; you can walk in, and the flowering weeks in March smell best.

spots.name: Badangia Waterfall
spots.note: Wider fall past the coffee gardens with a rough last kilometre; take a local for the turn off, it is easy to drive past.

name: Debrigarh (Hirakud Reservoir)
tagline: Gaur and leopard on the Hirakud reservoir shoreline

why.winter: Dec-Feb is peak: gaur herds out on the grasslands, big rafts of migratory waterfowl and 11-28 C days.
why.summer: April to June crosses 45 C here; animals do crowd the last waterholes but the jeep ride is punishing.
why.monsoon: Safaris stop through Jul-Sep as the tracks turn to slush and the reservoir backs up over the shoreline.
why.autumn: October is humid and green with poor sighting odds; things sharpen up from the first week of November.

vibe: Lakeside nature-camp tents run by forest staff; boat safaris, birders and school groups, no backpackers
hub: About 40 km from Sambalpur over the Hirakud dam and right dyke to the Dhodrokusum gate; camp pickup

spots.name: Hirakud Dam
spots.note: The long earthen dam that made this lake, with Gandhi Minar at one end for the reservoir view; drive the dyke road at dusk.

spots.name: Cattle Island
spots.note: A drowned hilltop in the reservoir grazed by feral cattle; forest boats run out from the camp jetty, roughly two hours return.

spots.name: Samaleswari Temple
spots.note: Sambalpur's presiding goddess on the Mahanadi bank, busiest at the evening aarti; easy to fold into the drive back to town.

spots.name: Huma Leaning Temple
spots.note: Shiva temple on the Mahanadi that leans well off vertical; boatmen row you to the sandbanks when the river is low.

name: Deomali
tagline: Odisha's highest peak at 1672 m above a sea of cloud

why.winter: Dec-Feb the summit drops near 4 C at dawn with an inversion filling the valleys; carry a real jacket.
why.summer: Mar-May is hazy and dusty with washed-out views, though the top still runs 8-10 C cooler than Koraput.
why.monsoon: Jun-Sep the last hairpins are fog and running mud, the camp shuts and the view is a wall of grey.
why.autumn: October gives the clearest air of the year and grass still green from the rain; the best sunrises here.

vibe: A tented nature camp near the top and dhaba villages below; bikers and Odia weekenders, no foreign faces
hub: 70 km from Koraput via Semiliguda by shared jeep or hired bike; the last climb is steep and unsealed

spots.name: Semiliguda
spots.note: The coffee and pepper town where the Deomali road turns off; last fuel, food and shared jeeps before the unsealed climb.

spots.name: Pottangi
spots.note: Coffee, pepper and pineapple country on the highway south of Semiliguda; roadside stalls sell the local beans by the kilo.

name: Duduma Falls (Machkund)
tagline: Machkund river hurls itself 175 m off the Eastern Ghats plateau

why.winter: Dec-Feb is comfortable at 12-28 C and the drop still impressive after good rains, though the hydel intake thins it weekly.
why.summer: March-June the Machkund is mostly diverted into the turbines and the 175 m wall shrinks to threads inside the heat haze.
why.monsoon: Jul-Aug the fall is at maximum fury but ghat roads from Koraput slide and fog swallows the gorge; September starts to pay.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the window: peak flow in washed post-monsoon air, and the drive down past Jalaput reservoir at its greenest.

vibe: Chai stalls, a railed viewpoint and hydel-township quiet; Odia and Araku day-trippers at noon, empty by late afternoon.
hub: Hired-car day trip, 2.5-3 h of ghat road from Jeypore or Koraput via Nandapur; nowhere to sleep at the falls.

spots.name: Jalaput Dam
spots.note: The Machkund reservoir that feeds the falls, half of it in Andhra; a quiet lake road with no shops, so carry water.

spots.name: Onukudelli Thursday Market
spots.note: Thursday haat where Bonda and Gadaba women come down from the hills; get there by 9 am and ask before you photograph anyone.

name: Gopalpur
tagline: Sleepy colonial beach town, quiet alternative to Puri

why.winter: Quiet, cool and empty: the best months for walking the lighthouse beach without Puri crowds.
why.summer: Increasingly hot and humid through May; the beach empties out almost entirely.
why.monsoon: Rough seas and heavy rain make the beach unusable for most of the season.
why.autumn: Weather turns pleasant by November; October can still carry monsoon leftovers.

vibe: Old lighthouse, empty sand, not much else after dark - solitude, not a scene.
hub: Nearest hub Berhampur, 30min auto; 6hr from Bhubaneswar.

spots.name: Gopalpur Lighthouse
spots.note: Red and white tower over the fishing beach; the climb gives you the whole coast, and visitors are let up in the afternoon only.

spots.name: Rushikulya River Mouth
spots.note: Mass olive ridley nesting beach; the turtles land around February and the hatchlings run in April, no torches or flash at night.

spots.name: Taratarini Temple
spots.note: Twin sister goddesses on a hill above the Rushikulya, reached by 999 steps or a ropeway; Tuesdays in Chaitra are packed.

spots.name: Potagarh Fort
spots.note: Ruined 18th century fort by the river at Ganjam town; empty ramparts in the scrub, no ticket, no shade and no signboards.

spots.name: Aryapalli Beach
spots.note: Casuarina backed sand where Berhampur families picnic; no shacks and no lifeguards, so carry water and stay out of the surf.

name: Gupteswar Caves (Koraput)
tagline: Limestone cave shrine above the Sabari river in old sal forest
festival: Feb/Mar: Maha Shivratri mela at the cave

why.winter: Nov-Feb is dry and 12-28 C: the Sabari runs low and clear below the cliffs and the bat-heavy cave stays cool, not clammy.
why.summer: April-May pushes 40 C down in the valley and the sal browns off; a dawn visit works, but the plateau towns feel far better.
why.monsoon: Shravan (Jul-Aug) fills the site with barefoot Bol Bom pilgrims and the swollen Sabari runs mud-brown; the steps get slick.
why.autumn: October is the sweet spot, monsoon-green forest and a full river, with the big Shivratri crowds still four months away.

vibe: A temple hamlet under huge sal trees, sadhus and Odia picnic parties; no stay worth the name, so base in Jeypore.
hub: Day trip from Jeypore, 55 km west by hired car, buses are rare; slow trains reach Jeypore, Koraput Jn 80 km.

spots.name: Sabari River
spots.note: The river below the cave steps marks the Chhattisgarh line; pilgrims bathe at the ghat, no boats and no shops past the lane.

name: Khandadhar Falls
tagline: A 244 m horsetail fall in the Bonai hills near Rourkela

why.winter: December still runs well; by Jan-Feb the flow thins but the pool is clear and the 2 km walk in is cool.
why.summer: By March to May the Korapani stream is a thin ribbon and the sal forest hits 42 C; not worth the drive.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the fall is enormous and the last fair-weather stretch turns to red slush and slip-prone rock.
why.autumn: October is the payoff: full flow, clean air and the forest still green after the rain pulls back.

vibe: Forest-department cottages and tents at the base; local picnic parties at weekends, tourists almost never
hub: 104 km from Rourkela via Bonaigarh, the last stretch rough forest road, then 2 km on foot

spots.name: Bonaigarh
spots.note: Last real town before the forest road, with fuel, ATMs and the only hotels; buses from Rourkela end here, then it is a jeep.

name: Khiching (Kichakeswari Temple)
tagline: Bhanja capital where a black chlorite temple was rebuilt stone by stone

why.winter: Dec-Feb dawns near 11 C and the black stone warms slowly; you get the temple courtyard, the sculpture shed and the ruin mounds alone.
why.summer: March still works before 9 am. April climbs past 40 C and May bakes Mayurbhanj with no shade between the mounds, so leave it alone.
why.monsoon: June is hot and dusty until the rains land; Jul-Sep greens the paddy, fills the old tanks and wets the carving, but buses from Karanjia crawl and the lanes turn to mud.
why.autumn: Oct-Nov is the pick: clear light on the chlorite, fields cut, cool enough to walk the whole scattered site in one morning.

vibe: A village of tank bunds and broken shrines; you sleep in a lodge or the government rest house and eat rice plates by the bus stand
hub: Bus from Karanjia, 25 km, or Baripada 150 km; nearest railhead Rairangpur, about 70 km of slow road

name: Konark
tagline: 13th-century Sun Temple: a UNESCO stone chariot in rock
festival: Dec: Konark Dance Festival

why.winter: Best light on the Sun Temple's stone wheels, and December's Dance Festival draws top performers.
why.summer: Stone courtyards get scorching by midday. Visit at dawn or skip Apr-Jun altogether.
why.monsoon: Humid and wet with little shade around the complex. An uncomfortable half-day visit.
why.autumn: Comfortable temperatures return by November. Good timing to combine with Puri.

vibe: A half-day monument stop for most; stay overnight for December's dance festival.
hub: 35km/1hr from Puri by shared auto or bus; easy day trip.

spots.name: Chandrabhaga Beach
spots.note: Dune beach where the Magha Saptami bathers gather in February; come for sunrise, then the temple before the buses land at ten.

spots.name: Konark Archaeological Museum
spots.note: Sculpture rescued from the ruins, including pieces never put back on the temple; small ticket, closed Friday, ten minutes away.

spots.name: Ramachandi Temple
spots.note: Goddess shrine where the Kushabhadra meets the sea, the standing stop on the marine drive; fried fish stalls by the crossing.

spots.name: Kuruma Buddhist Site
spots.note: Excavated monastery and a seated Buddha in a village off the Puri road; a caretaker opens it, allow half an hour and no more.

spots.name: Kakatpur Mangala Temple
spots.note: Maa Mangala by the Prachi, where priests wait for the dream that finds the Jagannath logs; Tuesdays bring the biggest queues.

spots.name: Chaurasi Varahi Temple
spots.note: Tantric shrine to the boar headed Varahi in a Prachi valley village; ask in Chaurasi for the priest, he keeps the key.

name: Koraput
tagline: Eastern Ghats coffee town of tribal markets and mist
festival: Dec: Parab tribal dance festival

why.winter: Dec-Feb mornings sit near 13 C at 870 m with mist over the coffee and pepper plots; dry, clear and cheap.
why.summer: Mar-May tops out near 33 C, hot for the Eastern Ghats but mild by Odisha standards, and hazy with dust.
why.monsoon: Jun-Aug the ghats are fog-bound and the hill roads to Deomali and Duduma get slick and often washed out.
why.autumn: October is the best month: the Kolab valley is green and Duduma still in spate; Parab follows in December.

vibe: Slow tribal-district town with cheap hotels and a Jagannath temple; travellers arrive off the Araku train
hub: Koraput Junction is on the Vizag-Kirandul line, a slow 7-8 h climb; buses from Jeypore and Rayagada

spots.name: Sabara Srikhetra Jagannath Temple
spots.note: Hilltop Jagannath temple open to everyone, unlike Puri, with a tribal museum in the same compound; shut in the afternoon.

spots.name: Upper Kolab Dam
spots.note: Reservoir above town with a boating jetty and a park by the spillway; the dam road is open in daylight hours only.

spots.name: Kolab Botanical Garden
spots.note: Terraced garden below the dam, empty on weekdays and full of picnic parties on Sunday; small ticket, gates close by dusk.

spots.name: Kunduli Friday Market
spots.note: Big Friday tribal haat where hill villages trade millet, mahua and forest produce; be there before noon, it thins out by two.

spots.name: Bagra Waterfall
spots.note: Wide low falls on the Kolab where Jeypore comes to picnic; best just after the monsoon, the rocks are slick and unrailed.

name: Mangalajodi (Chilika Wetlands)
tagline: Ex-poacher guides row you into Chilika's winter clouds of waterbirds

why.winter: Nov-Feb well over a lakh ducks, godwits and crakes pack the reedy channels; punts glide within metres and dawns are 12-15 C.
why.summer: March empties out fast as the migrants leave; April-May is a 40 C glare on open marsh with resident jacanas and little else.
why.monsoon: June is the worst heat of the year here; Jul-Sep the channels flood deep and boating turns iffy, resident breeders only.
why.autumn: October brings the first pintail and godwit flocks down from Siberia; by mid-November the full winter spectacle is on.

vibe: Bird photographers and a couple of community-run eco lodges; boatmen who once poached eggs now call crakes for you.
hub: Bhubaneswar airport 70 km via NH16, buses drop at Tangi 5 km out; slow trains stop at Kalupada Ghat 8 km away.

spots.name: Kalijai Temple
spots.note: Island shrine to the girl the lake took while crossing to her wedding; boats go from Barkul or Balugaon, an hour each way.

spots.name: Barkul
spots.note: The west shore jetty where the Chilika boats start; fix the rate before you board and stay for the sunset over the water.

spots.name: Balugaon
spots.note: Chilika's fish town on the highway, crab and prawn sold off the roadside each morning; the eateries cook what you point at.

name: Nrusinghanath (Gandhamardan Hills)
